note: An archive using the ZIP64 extensions, which section 7 requires every reader to accept. The other four .vnz cases are plain archives, so until this file existed an implementation could omit its extra-field parser entirely and pass every tier. WHERE THE MASKING IS APPLIED IS THE WHOLE POINT OF THE FILE. Python's `force_zip64` masks the LOCAL header only and leaves the central directory holding real 32-bit values; almost every reader takes sizes and offsets from the central directory, so a fixture built that way never asks the extra-field parser anything and stays green with the parser disabled - which is how this gap was found, by red-proofing a ZIP64 test and watching it pass. So this archive does the reverse: the local headers carry true values and the CENTRAL DIRECTORY masks compressed size, uncompressed size and local-header offset to 0xFFFFFFFF, moving all three into a ZIP64 extended-information extra field. Do not 'simplify' it by masking the local header instead, and do not regenerate it with a stock zip library, which will decline to emit ZIP64 for a 519-byte archive and quietly hand back a plain one. It catches TWO independent gaps and a red does not say which, so red-proof them separately: disable the central-directory extra-field parser, and separately ignore the ZIP64 end-of-central-directory record, whose locator is the only way to find the directory here because the plain end record masks its offset, its size and its entry counts. Entries are STORED rather than deflated because deflate has no canonical output and this archive is written by hand, so deflating it would make its bytes reproducible only in Go. Verified against three independent readers - Python's zipfile, Go's archive/zip and unzip - because a hand-built archive that only its own author can read proves nothing. This archive is INPUT, not an example of section 7.1's writer output: 7.1 says a conforming writer does not write ZIP64 records at all, and section 7 says a reader must read them anyway. That asymmetry is the reason this file has to be hand-built rather than produced by any library here. The root document is deliberately not the first entry. At local-header offset 0 a reader that loses the offset entirely and defaults to zero still finds the document, so the masked offset would be untested on the one entry that matters - a lost value that happens to be correct is not a test. `attachments/first.txt` exists only to push doc.vnx off zero, and moving it after the document, or deleting it, removes the property. Measured: with the extra field ignored and a lost offset defaulting to zero, doc.vnx reads as 0 bytes rather than as itself.
